report:
Based on this research, here's my report:

**Conclusion: Largely supported, with important caveats.**

The evidence generally backs the claim, primarily because opening a window/door lowers bedroom CO2 concentration, which correlates with better sleep. A key randomized controlled trial (Strøm-Tejsen et al., 2016, published in *Indoor Air*) found that when bedroom CO2 was reduced by opening a window (pilot: ~2,585 ppm vs. ~660 ppm), both objectively measured sleep quality and perceived air freshness improved significantly, along with next-day sleepiness, concentration, and logical reasoning scores ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168/)).

A 2023 field study from DTU (Denmark) reinforced this: reducing ventilation so CO2 rose from 856 to 1,927 ppm produced shorter deep sleep, longer light sleep, and more awakenings, while good ventilation (CO2 <750 ppm) prevented air-quality-related sleep disruption ([dtu.dk](https://www.dtu.dk/english/newsarchive/2023/05/ventilate-your-bedroom-at-night-you-perform-better-the-next-day)). Related 2023–2024 studies (MDPI, ScienceDirect) similarly found CO2 levels above ~1,000 ppm degrade sleep quality, supporting ventilation via open windows/doors as a mechanism ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2075-5309/13/11/2768), [sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132323011459)).

**Caveats:** Benefits depend on outdoor conditions—if outdoor air is polluted, cold, noisy, or allergen-laden, opening a window can worsen sleep or health rather than help it. A DTU field intervention across 40 real bedrooms found window/door opening improved indoor air quality, but effects vary by season and location ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132322008605)).

**Bottom line:** The core mechanism—reducing CO2 buildup improves sleep—is well-supported by controlled studies, but the practical benefit of opening a window specifically depends on outdoor air quality, temperature, and noise.
